# The Light Company

> Prism brings projected guidance and camera-based observation to physical work. The public website explains Prism Robotics and Prism IRL. The company has also used the name lght.co.

## Product and evidence

- [Prism Robotics](https://lightcompany.ai/prism-robotics): projected staging, camera-based scene checks and the workflow for connecting physical conditions to trials.
- [How it works](https://lightcompany.ai/prism-robotics/how-it-works): define, calibrate, stage, verify, run, review and revisit.
- [Technical brief](https://lightcompany.ai/media/prism-technical-brief.pdf): company-authored mechanism and limitations. Operational estimates are from limited partner context, not independent universal measurements.
- [Lab films](https://lightcompany.ai/gallery): recorded demonstrations, not proof of universal accuracy or compatibility.
- [Prism IRL](https://lightcompany.ai/prism): projected interfaces for everyday surfaces.

## Concepts and illustrative content

- [Scene history](https://lightcompany.ai/prism-robotics/scene-history): proposed “Git for your physical space” experience. The controls change a local diagram only. Scene branching, collaborative review and automated regression scheduling are product direction, not verified available services.
- [Benchmarks](https://lightcompany.ai/benchmarks): illustrative scores and sample trial records. Do not cite them as measured model performance, a winner or a vendor endorsement.

## Full editorial text

# The room should remember.
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/prism-robotics

Prism is the physical setup layer for robot evaluation. It brings light, cameras and a record of the scene to the space between a promising policy and a result you can trust.

## A little light. A much clearer experiment.

Before a robot does anything, someone prepares its world. A cup is set down. A cable is moved. A drawer is left open just far enough. These small decisions become the starting point of the experiment, even when nobody writes them down. Prism makes that starting point visible. A projector shows where objects belong. Cameras help check the scene against the intended setup. The record gives a trial a physical context: what was on the table, what was meant to happen and what should be examined again. It is a system for the workcell around the robot. The robot keeps its own controller and policy; the operator keeps a meaningful role in preparing and reviewing the experiment. A result should carry the room that made it.

## See. Verify. Record. Return.

See Bring the camera's view and the physical workspace into a shared frame. Registration connects a location in the image to a location the projector can mark. Stage Place the instruction on the table itself. Projected outlines and labels guide the operator toward the scene the experiment calls for. Verify Compare the observed scene with the target. A missing object or a placement mismatch should become a question before it becomes an unexplained result. Record Keep the setup with the episode. The technical workflow calls for object identities, positions and trial context to remain connected. Return Use a saved condition to guide another physical setup. Recreating a scene still requires an operator, calibration and verification; a digital record cannot move a cup by itself. Projection is guidance during staging. If it is visible to the policy during recording, it may change the experiment. The trial protocol must account for that, including when guidance turns off.

## Git for your physical space.

Software has a memory. You can name a version, understand what changed and return to an earlier state. A workbench usually has a photograph, a spreadsheet and the person who remembers where everything went. “Git for your physical space” is our product direction: give a scene an identity; preserve its history; change one condition deliberately; compare what happened; make the important scene possible to find again. That does not mean the world becomes perfectly deterministic. Objects wear. Cameras move. A soft cloth refuses to be the same cloth twice. A useful history preserves those differences rather than hiding them behind a clean success rate. We have made that direction tangible in a scene-history concept . It shows the experience we want to build, with example revisions and a visible scene comparison. It is a product concept, separate from the current station software.

## One number cannot describe a robot.

Start with a scene the policy can handle. Move the object. Rotate it. Introduce a distractor. Substitute an object. Change the light. One variable at a time gives the experiment a question you can actually answer. The aim is a capability map : a picture of where the policy works, where it becomes uncertain and where it breaks under the conditions you tested. The gaps matter too. An untested condition should stay untested, rather than borrowing confidence from a neighboring cell. Prism's projected staging directly helps with placement on a calibrated surface. Object choice, lighting, robot state and other conditions still need their own controls and records. See the capability-map guide for a practical way to structure the experiment.

## Built around the real workcell.

A Prism setup brings together a projector, a camera, local compute, a calibrated workspace and the operator preparing the scene. The exact mounting, field of view and camera-to-projector relationship matter. Good software cannot repair a loose mount by describing it more confidently. The process begins with the actual task: the objects, the reachable surface, the robot's view and what the team needs to compare. We discuss those conditions before proposing a station or an integration. The platform story grows from that physical foundation. Records are useful when their calibration and task context remain attached. Comparisons are useful when the policies faced comparable conditions. A replay is useful when the recreated scene has been checked again. Walk through an evaluation, from first setup to review .

## Ambition, with the evidence beside it.

The lab films show projected guidance and real workcells. Our technical brief describes initial-condition control, camera checks, episode logging and re-projection, along with the limits that still need to be measured. These are different kinds of evidence. A film demonstrates an interaction; it does not establish a placement tolerance or a universal improvement in policy performance. The brief's operational estimates come from a limited partner context, not a cross-industry study. The public benchmark workspace currently uses illustrative data to show the intended analysis experience. It is not a measured ranking of model providers. Scene branching, collaborative history and automated regression scheduling on this site are proposed direction unless explicitly identified otherwise.

## Questions worth asking.

Is Prism a simulator? Prism Robotics is centered on physical workcells. Simulation can help explore possible conditions; a physical evaluation still needs its own setup, observation and evidence. The website's examples and interactive concept do not run physical trials. Does it reset the world automatically? Projected targets guide a person in restoring the scene. Camera checks can help verify the result. Automatic object manipulation or perfect reconstruction of every scene is not a promise of this product page. Does it decide whether a task succeeded? Scoring requires an explicit rubric and review process. The broader platform direction includes model-assisted review, but scene verification and outcome scoring answer different questions. A correctly placed cup can still be grasped unsuccessfully. Can our team try it? Tell us about your workcell or register interest in a station . We will discuss fit, scope and availability directly. The interest form does not take payment or reserve a delivery date.

# Before the robot moves, make the scene legible.
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/prism-robotics/how-it-works

An evaluation begins before the first action and ends after the final score. Prism's job is to keep the physical setup connected to everything that follows.

## First, decide what the trial means.

Name the task in terms someone else can recognize. “Put the mug in the tray” is a start. Does the handle matter? Must the mug remain upright? Is contact with another object a failure? What happens when a camera loses the view? Write the success rule, the timeout, the allowed intervention and the reasons a trial may be invalid. Freeze them before comparing policies. A better reset does not resolve an ambiguous rubric.

## Give light and vision a common frame.

The projector and camera see the same workspace from different places. Registration connects their views so an instruction lands where it belongs. Mounting, focus, exposure, surface geometry and the usable field of view all affect the result. Check that relationship against the actual table. Keep a calibration reference with the setup. If the camera, projector or table moves, re-check the registration before treating an old scene as reproducible. Acceptance tolerances belong to the task; this site does not claim a universal accuracy figure.

## Put the instruction where the hands are.

Choose the target condition. The projector marks placement guides on the work surface, and the operator brings the physical objects into the scene. The instruction is shared: the person preparing the table and the person reviewing the trial can refer to the same intended arrangement. Light becomes an instruction in the place the work happens. Recorded Prism staging footage; playback does not control a robot. For a planar rigid object, an outline can communicate location and some orientation. It cannot fully specify the folds of a towel, the friction of a surface or the contents of an opaque container. Those conditions need additional controls.

## Check the scene before asking the policy a question.

Compare the camera observation with the target condition. The useful outcome is not a decorative green light; it is an understandable decision about whether this setup is acceptable for this trial. Keep the intended condition, observed placement and unresolved mismatch distinct. When the scene cannot be verified, preserve that uncertainty and resolve it before including the episode in a comparison. Detection confidence alone is not a physical guarantee.

## Let the trial happen under its declared conditions.

Once the operator accepts the setup, the robot runs through its own execution system. Guidance must be handled consistently: projected marks visible to the policy may become an unintended cue. Decide when they disappear, and verify that behavior in the recording. Record the policy or checkpoint identity, robot configuration, relevant sensor settings, condition identifier and any intervention. Preserve a failed trial as carefully as a successful one. A failure is often the most useful thing the experiment produces.

## Keep the reason beside the result.

Review the outcome against the declared rubric. Link the observation or recording that supports the decision, and separate setup-invalid episodes from policy failures. If a reviewer changes a score, keep the reason for the change. This is the intended evidence chain for a useful evaluation system. Specific recording formats, scoring integrations and review workflows must be agreed for a deployment; the public website is not an API specification.

## Make the interesting scene possible to find again.

When a new checkpoint arrives, return to a saved condition and stage it again. Re-check the physical state; do not assume yesterday's calibration and today's table are identical. Compare the new episode with the earlier one and keep the context of both. The long-term product direction is a shared history of scenes and results. Explore the interactive scene-history concept or use the evaluation planning guide to prepare a first experiment.

# Git for your physical space.
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/prism-robotics/scene-history
Status: proposed concept, not a connected product.

A place can have a past. A test can have a lineage. A failure can become a scene your whole team knows how to find.

## Save the condition, not just a picture.

A photograph can remind you what a table looked like. A useful scene record should also explain what mattered: the objects, target arrangement, calibration, task, policy and acceptance rules. It should distinguish what the system observed from what a person intended. Our proposed scene history gives that context a stable identity. A trial refers back to a scene revision, so the result does not become detached from its starting point when a video moves folders or someone renames a spreadsheet.

## Change one thing. Keep the question clear.

Imagine branching from a known scene to test a new object position. The baseline remains available. The branch makes the intended difference explicit, and the comparison asks a specific question: did this policy still succeed when the cup moved? Position, orientation, clutter, objects and lighting are useful experimental axes. They do not all have the same physical controls. A future workflow should make both the intended change and the limits of its verification visible.

## A difference you can point to.

The proposed comparison view brings two conditions and their episodes together. The reviewer sees what changed in the setup, which policy ran and what evidence supports the result. A changed rubric or camera configuration should be visible alongside a changed object position. The goal is a conversation with fewer missing pieces: “this is the scene,” “this is the change,” “this is what we observed.”

## Return to the question that mattered.

A physical replay would take a saved condition and project the staging instructions again. An operator restores the objects. The station checks what it can observe. The next trial gets its own record, linked to the earlier condition. Replay is a reconstruction, not time travel. The table may be the same while friction, wear, exposure or a deformable object differs. The product should help the team see those boundaries.

## The lab's memory, shared.

Beyond individual scene records, we are exploring collaborative review, named test suites, scheduled regression runs and a history of why a result was accepted or questioned. These are product directions shown here to make the ambition concrete; this page does not announce their availability. The measure of success is human: a new researcher should be able to understand an old failure without finding the one person who was in the room. Help shape the scene-history workflow or read the thinking behind physical version control .

# Intelligence belongs where life happens.
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/company

We spend our days teaching machines about the world. We are building a way for the world to answer back.

## The space beyond the screen.

Much of computing lives in a rectangle. Physical work happens elsewhere: on a bench, beside a machine, around a kitchen table, in the space a hand is about to reach. Light can meet that work where it is. A projected outline can tell a person where to place an object. A camera can help determine whether it arrived. Together, they make an interface that shares the surface with the task. That is the starting point for Prism. We want intelligence to become easier to see, question and use in the physical world.

## One idea, two places to begin.

Prism Robotics Robot evaluation needs a physical setup that can be described, checked and revisited. Prism Robotics brings projected staging and camera-based verification to that work, with a broader direction toward a shared history of scenes and results. Prism IRL Prism IRL explores information and interaction on everyday surfaces. The interface comes into the room: guidance where the hands are, information where the object is, light that helps a person act.

## What we want the work to feel like.

Legible. A person should understand what the system is asking, what it saw and what it still does not know. Grounded. Real footage, real materials and real operating constraints should shape the product. The workbench gets a vote. Open to correction. A failed trial, an uncertain observation or a disagreement is part of the record. Good tools make those moments easier to examine. Generous to the next person. Knowledge should survive a shift change. An experiment should be understandable to someone who was not there.

## Build the next layer with us.

This work sits across optics, perception, robotics, software and interaction design. It rewards people who can move between a careful explanation and a stubborn physical problem. For prospective colleagues Show us something you have made, studied or learned to see differently. Explore working together → For investors Explore the company thesis and the opportunity around physical AI evaluation. Read the investor overview → For labs and partners Bring a concrete task. We will start with the scene you need to understand. Start a conversation →

# Build something you can point to.
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/careers

A beam lands on a table. A camera notices a difference. A person understands what to do next. Making that moment useful takes many kinds of minds.

## The problems are wonderfully physical.

We care about the distance between a compelling demo and a tool someone uses again tomorrow. A calibration that survives the day. A record someone can understand six months later. An interface that remains clear when the room is noisy and the operator is tired. Those problems do not belong to one discipline. The best answer may involve a mount, a camera setting, a database record, a sentence or a better question.

## Where your curiosity might fit.

Perception & robotics Registration, scene understanding, evaluation methods and the boundaries of what a camera can verify. Systems & software Reliable station software, understandable records, integrations and tools that help a lab recover from mistakes. Optics & hardware Light, cameras, mounting, thermal behavior and the practical details that turn a workbench into a dependable instrument. Design & storytelling Interfaces that explain their own state; films and writing that make physical intelligence tangible without overstating it. Lab operations Repeatable processes, clear documentation and patient observation of the difference between intended and actual work.

## Bring a point of view and something to show.

A project, a repository, a paper, a physical build, a short film or a careful write-up can tell us how you think. Explain what you tried, what surprised you and what you would change. We welcome different educational and professional paths. If a conventional résumé leaves out the most interesting part of your work, tell us that part.

## Start with the work.

Email hi@lightcompany.ai with a short introduction, relevant links and the kind of contribution you want to make. Tell us your location and any practical constraints you want us to consider. Please do not send identity documents, financial information or sensitive information about other people. If a formal opportunity opens, its responsibilities, location and terms will be discussed explicitly. We cannot promise a response or a role from an expression of interest. Need an accessible way to share your work? Say what would help. Read our privacy notice for how contact information is handled.

Include the task, the robot or platform, the objects involved and the part of the evaluation that is hard to repeat. Tell us whether you are exploring, planning a pilot or already operating a lab. ## See the physical work.

Writing can explain a method. Footage shows what a person actually does with it. Explore the lab gallery , watch the evaluation film or follow the Prism workflow from staging to review. Operational figures in that brief reflect a limited partner context, not an independently validated market-wide benchmark.

## Reading that shaped the questions.

Robot Learning as an Empirical Science: Best Practices for Policy Evaluation argues for richer reporting of initial conditions, success criteria and observed behavior. Colosseum explores robustness across environmental changes in simulation. SIMPLER studies simulated evaluation against real robot setups. These are independent research projects, not Light Company results or endorsements. Our guides connect those questions to the practical work of preparing and documenting a physical scene. They do not turn a simulated result into a claim about a physical deployment.

## Explore the product direction.

The scene-history concept explores the idea of “Git for your physical space.” Its controls operate a diagram, not a station. For a concise machine-readable overview, see llms.txt and the public agent guide . They preserve the same distinction between demonstrated work and proposed direction.

# How to plan a real-world robot evaluation
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/resources/robot-evaluation

A robot evaluation is a carefully bounded question. The task, the scene and the rules decide what the answer can mean.

## Start with the decision.

Are you choosing between two checkpoints, testing whether a new object breaks a skill, or deciding whether a workflow is ready for a specific setting? These are different decisions. They deserve different experiments. Write the decision in one sentence. Then describe the evidence that would change your mind. This keeps a beautiful demonstration from quietly becoming a deployment claim. A practical example: “We want to know whether the new checkpoint improves placing this mug in this tray across the positions used at this workcell.” That question names the policy change, task, objects and scope. It leaves room to report what was not tested.

## Write the rules before the robot acts.

Define success in observable terms. Specify the time limit, allowed contact, acceptable final state and any permitted assistance. Decide how to handle interruptions, sensor loss, a bad reset or a stopped robot. Keep three outcomes separate: a valid success, a valid failure and an invalid or unresolved episode. A reset mistake should not silently count against the policy, and removing a difficult valid failure would make the report misleading. When two reviewers disagree, retain the disagreement and resolve it against the rubric. A scoring model can help organize review, but its answer still depends on the evidence and instructions it receives.

## Choose the world the policy will face.

List the conditions that matter: object identity, position, orientation, clutter, lighting, camera arrangement, robot start state and relevant surface properties. Choose which to hold fixed and which to vary deliberately. Begin with a baseline that can be described and restored. Then choose a schedule of conditions that answers the question. Repeating an easy scene many times does not establish performance across a wider set of scenes. Give every intended condition an identifier. Record what was actually staged and whether it met the acceptance rule. A projected target is useful, but the target is not proof that the object arrived there.

## Leave a record another person can follow.

At minimum, connect each episode to the task and rubric versions, policy or checkpoint identity, scene condition, robot configuration, outcome and any intervention. Where recordings are collected, preserve their relationship to the episode and handle access according to the team's data agreement. Here is a downloadable evaluation checklist . It is a planning aid, not a Prism API contract. What was the intended setup, and how was it checked? Which policy ran, with which robot and sensor configuration? Was projected guidance visible during the recording? What happened, and what evidence supports the score? Did anyone intervene, discard a trial or change a rule? Which conditions remain untested?

## Report the boundary of the result.

Give the number of trials and successes, the conditions covered, the uncertainty appropriate to the experiment and the reasons for exclusions. Explain the important failure modes in words. A single average can hide the condition that matters most to the team using the robot. Compare policies on a matched set of conditions where possible. Consider trial order and wear: running one candidate first all day and another after the objects or hardware have changed can introduce another difference. The Robot Learning as an Empirical Science: Best Practices for Policy Evaluation paper calls for more informative reporting than a bare success rate. This guide applies that principle to a workcell planning conversation; it does not prescribe a universally sufficient trial count. Next: why initial conditions belong in the result .

# Why robot evaluation starts with the reset
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/resources/initial-conditions

The robot's first observation is already the result of somebody's work. That work deserves a record.

## The smallest change in the room.

A mug returns to the table, almost where it was. The handle turns a little. A cable lies closer to the gripper. Nothing about the model changed, but its next observation did. That does not make variation a mistake. A capable robot must operate through variation. The problem is variation that enters the evaluation without being chosen, measured or described. When a team compares two policies, it needs to understand whether the policies faced comparable conditions. Otherwise a changed result may reflect a changed scene, a changed policy or both.

## Keep intention, observation and acceptance separate.

Intended condition The scene the protocol asks for: objects, target positions and other declared conditions. Observed condition What the camera or operator can actually establish about the prepared scene. Acceptance decision Whether the observed scene is suitable for this trial under the task's tolerances, including any unresolved uncertainty. Collapsing these into one “ready” flag makes the interface simple at the expense of the experiment. A useful system lets a reviewer recover the reason the trial was accepted.

## What projected staging changes.

Prism projects placement guidance onto the work surface so an operator can prepare a target condition without referring back and forth to a separate drawing. Camera registration connects the projected instruction to the observed workspace. The Prism technical brief describes this as an initial-condition layer: stage, verify, log and re-project a saved condition. It also identifies limits. Planar placement is easier to express than a complete three-dimensional configuration; deformable objects and lighting need additional treatment. Visible projected marks may themselves affect a vision policy. The recording protocol must specify when guidance is shown and when it is removed. “No tape on the table” is helpful only if the replacement does not introduce an unexamined cue.

## A reset worth repeating.

Start by naming the objects and the target arrangement. Check calibration against the actual workspace. Stage the scene, inspect the observation and record the acceptance decision. Only then begin the policy episode. When a reset cannot meet the requirement, preserve that fact. Do not quietly substitute a nearby scene while retaining the original condition label. When the table, camera or projector moves, re-check the relationship before using old targets. This is not a claim that every source of variability can be eliminated. It is a way to make the setup part of the experiment instead of an invisible assumption.

## Variation becomes useful when it has a name.

Once a baseline is understood, move beyond it deliberately. Change one axis and record it. Then test combinations where interactions matter. The resulting capability map can show where a policy's performance changes across the conditions tested. For background on richer physical evaluation reporting, see Robot Learning as an Empirical Science: Best Practices for Policy Evaluation . For the product workflow, see how Prism works .

# A capability map tells you where to look next
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/resources/capability-maps

An average tells you how often. A map helps you understand where, under what conditions and what to try next.

## The failure inside the average.

Imagine two policies with similar overall results. One works across the table but struggles with a particular object. The other handles that object well but fails near the edge of the workspace. A single number can make them look interchangeable. A capability map organizes outcomes by the condition that produced them. It lets a team ask a practical question: does this policy work in the part of the world we actually care about? The map is an account of tested conditions. It does not establish capability in every untested scene, and it is not a safety certification.

## Five useful questions for a physical scene.

Position What happens when the target moves across the reachable surface? Keep the camera and robot configuration recorded. Orientation What happens when the object turns? State which orientation is being varied and what can actually be verified. Clutter What happens when another object enters the scene? Record its identity and placement rather than calling everything “cluttered.” Objects What happens when the target changes? Size, material, shape and familiarity may change together; a substitution is rarely one perfectly isolated property. Lighting What happens when illumination changes? Record the lighting arrangement and relevant camera settings. Projected staging does not automatically control ambient light.

## Change one variable, then examine interactions.

Begin with one axis at a time. It makes a failure easier to attribute and gives the team a readable first map. If the cup moves while the camera and light also change, the result cannot isolate the effect of position. After the first pass, test combinations that matter. Clutter and orientation may interact. A policy that tolerates either change alone may fail when both occur. One-variable tests are a useful beginning, not a complete account of the world. Colosseum is a simulation research example of evaluating environmental perturbations systematically. Its findings are not Prism measurements; the useful lesson here is to make the axes of variation explicit.

## Let the blank cells stay blank.

Show trial counts alongside outcomes. Mark untested conditions clearly. Preserve invalid episodes and review disagreements separately. If one cell contains many trials and another contains only a few, the visual treatment should not suggest equal certainty. Keep the task, rubric, policy and condition versions attached to the map. Comparing maps made under different rules can create a persuasive picture of a change that was never actually measured. Our benchmark workspace uses illustrative data to explore this interface. It demonstrates the reading experience, not the performance of the model families shown.

## Use the map to choose the next experiment.

A useful map changes what the team does. It might reveal a narrow position boundary, motivate a new object test or identify a scene worth replaying against the next checkpoint. Preserve the conditions that led to that decision. Prism's role begins with making physical placement more explicit through projected guidance and camera checks. The broader ambition is to connect those scenes with the history of what the team learned. Read about physical version control or bring us a task to discuss .

# What should a physical scene remember?
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/resources/physical-version-control

A laboratory has a memory. Too much of it lives in the person who happened to be there.

## The day the person leaves the room.

The video still exists. The result is in the spreadsheet. But the person who set up the table remembers the detail that makes it meaningful: a camera was moved, an object was substituted, a trial was restarted after an interruption. When that memory disappears, the record becomes harder to use. A new researcher can watch what happened without knowing enough to ask the same question again. “Git for your physical space” names the product direction we are exploring with Prism. It borrows the idea of an intelligible history from software, while taking seriously how different the physical world is.

## A scene needs an identity.

A scene record should connect the intended arrangement with what was observed: object identities, positions, calibration reference and the conditions the task depends on. A trial should point back to that record, not merely to a folder with a familiar name. A revision then describes a change. The cup moved. The object changed. The lighting arrangement was different. The old condition remains understandable, and the new one explains its relationship to it. That relationship is the beginning of a useful comparison. It also makes missing information visible: a field can be unknown rather than silently assumed to match.

## The difference is the question.

In a physical experiment, a difference is not just something to display. It is often the reason to run the trial. Did the new policy improve on the old failure? Did changing the object reveal a dependency the team had not noticed? A useful history would keep the scene change, policy change and rubric change distinct. It would let someone review the evidence for the outcome and understand why a score was revised. The proposed scene-history interface makes a small part of this idea concrete. Its example revisions are illustrative and do not represent a connected lab or shipped collaboration system.

## Replay is a reconstruction.

Software can restore bytes exactly. A workcell cannot promise the same thing about friction, wear, exposure or the fold of a cloth. Projected guidance can help restore an arrangement; observation must still establish what was achieved. This is where the metaphor earns its limits. A scene history should not pretend to freeze the world. It should make the assumptions and tolerances of a reconstruction available for inspection. The Prism technical brief describes re-projecting a logged condition as a route to physical regression testing. Whether a specific task can be repeated closely enough remains something to measure in that task's setup.

## A record generous enough for someone else.

The destination is not a prettier archive. It is a lab where a failure remains findable, a comparison remains explainable and an old experiment can teach someone new. That asks for more than storage. It asks for names people understand, reasons kept beside decisions, permissions appropriate to the data and a way to say “we do not know” without breaking the workflow. The room cannot stand still. Its history can still make sense. Explore Prism Robotics , or tell us what your team's physical record is missing .

# What the browser remembers.
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/cookies

A small amount of browser state supports the website. Embedded services may have their own behavior.

## Storage used by the website

The benchmark introduction stores a dismissal flag in session storage under prism-benchmark-intro-v1 . It helps avoid repeatedly showing the same introduction during a browsing session. It does not contain your name or email. The scene-history concept has no saved account or server-side scene history. Its selected revision is held in the page while it is open. Reloading returns the example to its starting state. Hosting and security services may use cookies or similar mechanisms for delivery, abuse prevention or access controls. Their behavior can differ from the page's own scripts.

## Third-party content

The gallery uses YouTube's player technology. Loading that page or interacting with its player can contact YouTube and involve information such as your IP address and browser details. Third-party cookies and other processing are governed by the provider's settings and policies. Some older pages may request remotely hosted fonts. New company pages use locally hosted fonts. Following an external link takes you to a service with its own privacy practices.

## Your choices

You can remove cookies and site storage through your browser settings, block third-party cookies and choose not to load pages containing external media. Clearing storage may make an introduction appear again. The current website code does not include advertising pixels or a marketing analytics tracker. If additional non-essential tracking is introduced, its purpose and any required choices should be provided before it is used. For questions about personal information, see the privacy notice or contact hi@lightcompany.ai .

# Trust begins with a clear account.
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/trust

A tool that helps people examine evidence should be clear about its own boundaries. Here is where to start.

## The public website

The website explains our work, hosts films and educational content, and collects station-interest submissions. It is separate from a customer's operational workcell. The public scene-history concept does not connect to cameras or robot controllers. The station-interest endpoint validates submitted fields, limits request size, checks the request origin and stores accepted submissions in a database. Those are specific implementation measures, not a claim of comprehensive security certification. Read the privacy notice and browser-storage information for the public site's data practices.

## Before a station enters your lab

A deployment discussion should establish the data and operating boundaries before access is provided. These are questions to settle together, not a list of services this website promises: Which camera images, scene records and trial recordings are collected? What stays on the station, what is transmitted and where is it stored? Who can access the records, and how is access removed? How are updates, credentials, backups and incident contacts handled? What retention, export and deletion arrangements apply? Which actions require operator review, and which system controls the robot? Any customer-specific security commitments, data-processing terms, service levels or network requirements belong in the applicable written agreement.

## Claims you can inspect

We distinguish recorded demonstrations, workflow descriptions, operational estimates and proposed product concepts. None should silently stand in for another. The public benchmark scores are illustrative. Scene-history branching and collaborative workflows shown here are concepts. This site does not assert SOC 2, ISO 27001 or another certification, nor does it promise universal compatibility or a guaranteed accuracy level. For the physical method and known constraints, read the technical brief . For a proposed deployment, ask us for evidence relevant to your actual task.

## Report a security concern

Email hi@lightcompany.ai with “Security report” in the subject. Include the affected URL or component, a clear description and non-sensitive reproduction steps. Do not include credentials, private customer data or harmful payloads in the initial message. Avoid accessing data that is not yours or disrupting a live service. This page is a reporting contact, not authorization to test private systems or a promise of a bounty.

# An explanation should let people in.
Source: https://lightcompany.ai/accessibility

We want people to be able to understand our work without needing a particular device, way of seeing or way of interacting.

## How we approach the website

The company pages use semantic headings, visible keyboard focus, a skip link, readable contrast and responsive layouts. Interactive controls have text labels. Motion respects the browser's reduced-motion preference where supported by the page. The scene-history concept includes a text description of what changes, so its visual diagram is not the only explanation. The ASCII footer is decorative and is hidden from assistive technology. We use the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines as a reference for improvement. This statement is not a claim of complete conformance or an independent accessibility audit.

## Known limitations

Some recorded demonstrations communicate information visually, and not every video has a complete caption or audio-description track. Some older pages and third-party players may have different accessibility behavior from the new company pages. If a film, document or interactive view prevents you from getting the information you need, tell us which content matters. We can discuss a text explanation or another way to share it.

## Tell us where the experience breaks

Email hi@lightcompany.ai with the page URL, what you were trying to do and what happened. If useful, include your browser or assistive technology, but do not send sensitive personal information. We welcome specific reports about keyboard access, contrast, text size, motion, media alternatives or confusing controls. A useful website should remain useful when someone's way of using it differs from ours.
